text: My business is to use what does turn up with diligence and skill.
plain: You do not pick the roll of the dice. You play it well.

text: Like the hour I must be here and like an hour pass away.
plain: You are here for a while and then you are gone, like an hour of the day.

text: It is for you, then, to take what is given you and make the most of it.
plain: Take the hand you were dealt and make the most of it.

text: No tyrant ever took six months to execute a man, but a fever often takes a year to kill one.
plain: Death comes by a fever as easily as by a tyrant, so quit fearing the method.

text: What matters it to you, by what road you are to go down to Hades? All roads are alike.
plain: The road down is the same no matter how you go.

text: Who can compel you to think against your will?
plain: Nobody can force a thought into your head.

text: There is only one thing for you to remember, that is, the distinction between what is yours and what is not yours. Never lay claim to anything that is not your own.
plain: Sort what is yours from what is not, and never claim the second.

text: What then leads us to consult diviners so constantly? Cowardice, fear of events.
plain: We keep asking for forecasts because we are scared of what happens.

text: Each man is strengthened and preserved by the exercise of the functions that correspond to his nature, the carpenter by carpentering, the grammarian by studies in grammar.
plain: You become what you practice. The carpenter by carpentering.

text: Philosopher, where are those principles you were talking of? Whence did you fetch them forth to utter? From the lips and no further.
plain: Talking the talk is easy. Where are your principles when something goes wrong?

text: Do you think you must lose cash in order to suffer damage? Does no other sort of loss damage man? If you lost skill in grammar or music you would count the loss as damage; if you are going to lose honour and dignity and gentleness, do you count it as nothing?
plain: Losing money is not the only loss. Losing honor and self-respect costs more.

text: No one is evil without destruction and loss.
plain: Every bad act costs the person who does it something real.

text: The beginning of philosophy with those who approach it in the right way and by the door is a consciousness of one's own weakness and want of power in regard to necessary things.
plain: Wisdom starts when you admit how little power you have.

text: Our philosophers have precisely defined what a man must learn in order to know how to argue: but we are still quite unpractised in the proper use of what we have learnt.
plain: Everyone has learned the lessons. Almost nobody has practiced them.

text: In fact, where he has knowledge there he has confidence.
plain: Where you have done the work, you are not afraid.

text: Yet we are anxious for our bit of a body, for our bit of property, for what Caesar will think, but are not anxious at all for what is within us.
plain: We panic over our body, our stuff and what the boss thinks, and ignore our own character.

text: Why, no good man whines or groans or laments, no good man grows pale or trembles or says, 'How will he receive me? What hearing will he give me?'
plain: A steady person does not go pale over how someone else will receive him.

text: Miserable man, tell the truth and be not a braggart nor claim to be a philosopher. Know who are your masters. As long as you give them this hold over your body, you must follow every one who is stronger than you.
plain: If you let others hold power over your body and comfort, you will obey whoever is stronger.

text: May we, then, infer that in the sphere of conduct too it is not enough merely to wish to become good, but one must learn certain things?
plain: Wanting to be good is not enough. You have to study and train for it.

text: What are you doing, man? Not all decisions, but right decisions.
plain: Sticking to a bad decision is not strength. Check that it is right first.

text: But if you lay a rotten and crumbling foundation you will not be able to build even a tiny building; the more courses and the stronger that you lay upon it the quicker will it collapse.
plain: Building more on a bad foundation just makes the collapse faster.

text: May it never be my lot to have for friend a wise fool: nothing is more difficult to handle.
plain: A smart fool is the hardest friend to deal with.

text: Sit still and pray forsooth, that your rheum may not flow. Nay, wipe your nose rather and do not accuse God.
plain: Quit praying that the problem goes away. Wipe your nose and handle it.

text: But if we kept our fear not for death or exile, but for fear itself, then we should practise to avoid what we think evil.
plain: Fear fear itself, and you will learn to avoid what actually harms you.

text: The result of our want of practice is that we are always heaping up terrors and imagining things bigger than they really are.
plain: Untrained minds pile up terrors and blow everything out of proportion.

text: What is it alarms me? The sea? No, but my judgement about it.
plain: It is never the thing itself that scares you, it is what you think about it.

text: What, then, are the burdens that weigh upon us and drive us out of our minds? What else but our judgements?
plain: What crushes you is mostly your own judgment of events.

text: To guard what is your own, not to claim what is another's; to use what is given you, not to long for anything if it be not given; if anything be taken away, to give it up at once and without a struggle, with gratitude for the time you have enjoyed it, if you would not cry for your nurse and your mammy.
plain: Guard what is yours, use what you are given, and let go of what is taken without a fight.

text: Man, be bold at last, even to despair, as the phrase is, that you may have peace and freedom and a lofty mind. Lift up your neck at last, as one released from slavery.
plain: Be bold. Peace and freedom come when you stop cowering.

text: What would have become of Heracles, if he had stayed at home? He would have been Eurystheus, and no Heracles.
plain: Staying home safe makes you nobody.

text: Cleanse your own heart, cast out from your mind, not Procrustes and Sciron, but pain, fear, desire, envy, ill will, avarice, cowardice, passion uncontrolled.
plain: Clear your own mind of pain, fear, desire and envy before you try to fix the world.

text: If you wish for anything else, with groaning and sorrow you will follow what is stronger than you, ever seeking peace outside you, and never able to be at peace: for you seek it where it is not, and refuse to seek it where it is.
plain: You hunt for peace outside yourself, where it is not.

text: What is the first business of the philosopher? To cast away conceit: for it is impossible for a man to begin learning what he thinks he knows.
plain: You cannot learn what you think you already know.

text: Every habit and every faculty is confirmed and strengthened by the corresponding acts, the faculty of walking by walking, that of running by running. If you wish to have a faculty for reading, read; if for writing, write.
plain: You get better at a thing by doing it. Want to read more, read.

text: So if you lie in bed for ten days, and then get up and try to take a fairly long walk, you will see how your legs lose their power.
plain: Rest ten days and watch your legs forget what they could do.

text: So generally if you wish to acquire a habit for anything, do the thing; if you do not wish to acquire the habit, abstain from doing it, and acquire the habit of doing something else instead.
plain: To build a habit, do the thing. To kill one, replace it.

text: If, then, you wish not to be choleric, do not feed the angry habit, do not add fuel to the fire. To begin with, keep quiet, and count the days when you were not angry.
plain: Do not feed the angry habit. Count your calm days.

text: I used to be angry every day, then every other day, then every three days, then every four.
plain: Progress on anger is slow: every day, then every other, then every third.

text: But first of all do not be hurried away by the suddenness of the shock, but say, 'Wait for me a little, impression. Let me see what you are, and what is at stake: let me test you'.
plain: Pause before an impulse and ask what it really is.

text: Stay, unhappy man! be not carried away. Great is the struggle, divine the task; the stake is a kingdom, freedom, peace, an unruffled spirit.
plain: The fight is worth it: freedom, peace, a steady mind.

text: Take away the fear of death, and you may bring as much thunder and lightning as you will, and you will discover what deep peace and tranquillity is in your mind.
plain: Without the fear of death, any storm leaves you calm.

text: Show me one who is sick and yet happy, in peril and yet happy, dying and yet happy, in exile and happy, in disgrace and happy.
plain: Show me a man who stays happy in sickness, danger, exile or disgrace.

text: Wealth is not in our power, nor health, nor anything else, in a word, except the proper use of impressions.
plain: Money and health are not up to you. How you read events is.

text: The Governing Principle of the bad man is not to be trusted; it is uncertain, irresolute, conquered now by one impression, now by another.
plain: Do not trust anyone ruled by whatever impression hits them last.

text: But what can hinder the will? Nothing beyond the will, only the perversion of the will itself.
plain: Only your own will can stop your will.

text: Man, you are forgetting your purpose! You were not travelling to this, but through it.
plain: The comfortable stop on the road is not the destination.

text: What prevents you from being unfortunate, though you speak like Demosthenes? Though you can analyse syllogisms like Chrysippus, what prevents you from being wretched, mournful, envious—in a word, bewildered and miserable? Nothing prevents you.
plain: Polished words and clever skills do not make you any less miserable.

text: What makes a man beautiful? Is it the presence of a man's virtue? Therefore, young man, if you would be beautiful, make this the object of your effort, human virtue.
plain: Real beauty in a man is virtue, so work on that.

text: First get to know who you are, and then adorn yourself.
plain: Know who you are first. Then dress it up.

text: Did Socrates persuade all who came to him to attend to their characters? Not one in a thousand! Nevertheless when appointed to this post, as he says, by the ordinance of God, he refused to desert it.
plain: Socrates reached almost no one and kept at it anyway.

text: Unhappy man, even while you are learning this lesson you are in an agony of terror lest some one should think scorn of you, and you ask whether any one is talking about you!
plain: You say you are studying wisdom and you are still sweating over who is talking about you.

text: It is fitting for sailors who are in good trim to light a fire, and take their dinner, if luck serves, and to sing and dance: but you come to me when the ship is sinking and begin hoisting the topsails!
plain: Fancy theory is for calm seas. When the ship is sinking you need the basics.

text: Go out as soon as it is dawn and whomsoever you may see and hear, question yourself and answer as to an interrogator.
plain: Start the day by questioning what you see and what is up to you.

text: As it is, we are caught open-mouthed by every impression we meet, and only in the lecture-room, if then, does our mind wake up a little.
plain: We only think clearly in the classroom, and out in the street every impression catches us off guard.

text: What is faction, discord, criticism, accusation, irreligion, foolishness? All these are judgements, nothing else, and judgements passed on things beyond the will, as though they were good and evil.
plain: Most of your suffering is a judgment about things you cannot control.

text: The soul is like a dish full of water, and the impressions like the rays of light which strike the water. Now when the water is disturbed the light seems to be disturbed too, but it is not really disturbed.
plain: A disturbed mind makes everything seem disturbed, but the things themselves are fine.
